Eggs of the Great black-backed gull (Larus marinus) incubated under artificial conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], which is considered the optimal temperature for development in several related species, typically hatch after an incubation period of 27 days [ab = 27 days]. Newly emerged chicks have a wet weight at birth of approximately 80 grams [Wwb = approximately 80 grams], a relatively heavy mass for a larid hatchling, reflecting the large size of the egg and the substantial yolk reserves that support the chick through its first days of life. This initial body mass places the young among the largest of all gull chicks at hatching, an adaptation likely linked to the competitive pressures of the crowded colonial nesting environment where rapid early development is advantageous for survival and sibling dominance.

As the nestling phase progresses, the chicks undergo a period of rapid growth fueled by intensive biparental provisioning. By the time they fledge, which occurs approximately 52 days after hatching [tx = approximately 52 days after hatching] under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]), the young birds have increased their body mass substantially. The post-fledging period is a critical phase of nutritional independence and dietary transition, as the juvenile birds must learn to forage effectively on their own. The timing of fledging is constrained by the need to achieve flight feather maturation and sufficient muscle development to sustain powered flight, a milestone that in this species is reached at the upper end of the range reported for large gulls.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a protracted developmental trajectory. The attainment of sexual maturity, indicated by gonadal swelling and a surge in circulating testosterone, occurs at 156 days after hatching [tp = 156 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], although physiological changes can begin as early as 49 to 56 days. Despite this relatively early onset of reproductive maturity, first breeding is typically deferred until well after the bird has achieved full adult plumage and body size. The delay between puberty and actual nesting reflects the substantial energetic investment required for territory acquisition, pair bonding, and the establishment of a breeding site within the competitive social hierarchy of the colony.

The first brood occurs at 5 years since birth [tR = 5 years since birth] under the thermal conditions typical of this species' active metabolic range (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]), making this one of the later-maturing large gulls. Females typically produce a single clutch of between 1 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 5 eggs per clutch] annually, with exactly one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This maximum reproductive output is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity, given the high survival costs of chick rearing in a harsh coastal environment where food availability can be unpredictable. The investment in each egg is considerable, as the eggs are large relative to the female's body size and require substantial calcium reserves for shell formation.

The maximum lifespan of the Great black-backed gull in the wild has been documented at approximately 32.8 years [am = approximately 32.8 years] at the typical active body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a longevity that places this species among the longest-lived of all gulls. Adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of 1407 grams [Wwi = 1407 grams], while males, which are the larger sex, reach an ultimate wet weight of 1806 grams [Wwi = 1806 grams], representing one of the most pronounced sexual size dimorphisms within the genus Larus. The initial wet weight of the egg, approximately 116.5 grams [Ww0 = approximately 116.5 grams], represents a substantial investment by the parents and, when compared to the neonatal mass of approximately 80 grams [Wwb = approximately 80 grams], highlights the energetic cost of producing the calcareous shell and albumen that buffer the embryo during the 27-day incubation period.
